title: Leaving school after eighth grade, Boy Scouts and hospitality
summary: Green says he went as far as eighth grade, enjoyed performing for neighbours as Southern hospitality, and was educated by his aunt and the radio company school.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Well, in other words, you didn't continue with school after what point?
Well, I think I went as far as the eighth grade, see, because I did -- I became a Boy Scout and got in the Boy Scouts --
Well, what age range are you talking about now, when you used to do this composition in front of the class?
Well, it was on up until around when I was -- I guess I was going on nine years old, you see.
Uh-huh. So you've always enjoyed performing in front of the class?

Yeah, I enjoyed performing, period. I loved to, you know -- I didn't know as they would call it entertainment, you know, but, as I say, in the South that's a way of life is hospitality, you know. Like the family would send like their children to visit like their neighbors. Sometime the neighbors would be kind of old people. But regardless, it make no difference whether you're child or not, you'd have to know how to keep company, you know, like sit and listen to them talk or whatever they did.

But you'd have to be there as a visitor, you see?
And I guess that's how I got inspired to be a performer of some sort, you know, because I had been with the radio company, you

see, but my mother's mother made me throw that out of my mind, see. Well, if they don't want you to do what you enjoy doing mostly, why just don't go back, you see. So that's what happened, you see. And they were like guardians to me. I was a minor. And --

-- so as I say, you keep these people company, and they would always teach you something. You would always get some kind of reward for this. I mean the -- they'd fix you like a delicious meal or something or give you some kind of nice gift to take home to maybe your mother.
The neighbors, you know, like whoever you're keeping company with, you know.
I see. I see. So what happened? You were --
Tame became a natural ability, huh?
Let's go into that. So basically your composing in front of the class was for what reason? I mean what -- what meaning did it have in your life?

Well, it meant that I was -- eventually I was going to be smarter, more educated, more worldly, know more about the world, you see, and one part there when, after I got in the Boy Scouts, we had to go to school again. See, that's what when we went into geography, right?

As I say, one of my mother's mother's daughters was a teacher. She was studying to be a teacher, and she educated me a lot, you see. She used to teach me, you see? Also so I was fortunate in education because I was getting it from all these different directions.
Like when I was working for the American Broadcasting Company on the Children's Hour, they had a school that we went to, professional school, you see? And --
